To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

axoplasmic Na+ accumulation during chemical ischemia activates three distinct sources of Ca2+ release: (1) the Na+/Ca2 + exchanger, (2) ryanodine receptor channels, and (3 ) the phospholipase IP3 pathway.

Na+ influx is required for Ca2+ release from intracellular stores during chemical ischemia and that this release is mediated in part by mitochondrial Na+/Ca 2+ exchange, phospholipase-dependent production of IP3, and ryanodine receptor modulation.

the major source of Ca2+ accumulation during ischemia in optic nerve axons is Na+ influx, and that this Na+ influx activates three separate intracellular sources of Ca2+ that together contribute to the axonal injury.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which Na+ and Ca2+ accumulate in axons during chemical ischemia.
the mechanisms of Ca2+-induced injury in the optic nerve.
the mechanism of Ca2+ accumulation in the optic nerve during ischemia in vitro.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Na+-dependent Ca2+ accumulation in axons during ischemia involves a combination of mitochondrial and nonmitochondrial sources of Ca2+ release.
Na+ accumulation is a key factor in Ca2+ release from the three sources and that inhibition of any of these sources improves the recovery of axons from chemical ischemia.
the Na+-dependent Ca2+ accumulation in the ischemic optic nerve axon results from the activation of three Ca2+-releasing mechanisms that are not necessarily linked in series.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Na+ influx into axons is the primary trigger for axonal injury and that the Na+ influx is a result of a failure in axonal energy supply.
axons are exquisitely sensitive to the accumulation of intracellular Ca2+ and Na+, and these changes are interrelated.
axonal Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release is a significant contributor to Ca2+ overload and that blocking Na+-dependent Ca2+ release may be a useful strategy for neuroprotection during chemical ischemia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Ca2+ release from intracellular stores is a significant contributor to the Ca2+ rise that occurs during ischemia.
axonal Na+ accumulation is a key factor in the development of ischemia-induced Ca2+ overload in axons and that this accumulation is driven by Na+ influx.
the Na+/Ca2+-exchanger is a major contributor to Ca2+ release from intracellular stores during chemical ischemia.
